questions.question_text: An operating system contains 3 user processes each requiring 2 units of resource R. The minimum number of units of R such that no deadlocks will ever arise is
questions.explanation: With 3 processes each demanding 2 units, if any single process can be given its full demand, deadlock cannot occur. Using the worst-case formula (demand-1) summed over all processes plus one, 3 processes each needing 2 units require (2-1)+(2-1)+(2-1)+1 = 4 units to guarantee no deadlock.

questions.question_text: A computer has six tape drives, with n processes competing for them. Each process may need two drives. What is the maximum value of n for the system to be deadlock free?
questions.explanation: Each of the n processes needs 2 drives. With 6 drives total, if each of 5 processes is given 1 drive, at least one process can be given both drives it needs and complete execution, then release its drives for others to use, ensuring no deadlock. This works up to n = 5.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following is NOT a valid deadlock prevention scheme?
(a) Release all resources before requesting a new resource.
(b) Number the resources uniquely and never request a lower numbered resource than the last one requested.
(c) Never request a resource after releasing any resource
(d) Request and all required resources be allocated before execution.

options.label: A
options.text: Release all resources before requesting a new resource.

options.label: B
options.text: Number the resources uniquely and never request a lower numbered resource than the last one requested.

options.label: C
options.text: Never request a resource after releasing any resource

options.label: D
options.text: Request and all required resources be allocated before execution.

questions.explanation: Option (c) does not correspond to any standard deadlock prevention strategy; it neither breaks hold-and-wait, circular-wait, nor any other necessary condition, so it is not a valid scheme.

questions.question_text:
In a certain operating system, deadlock prevention is attempted using the following scheme. Each process is assigned a unique timestamp, and is restarted with the same timestamp if killed. Let P_h be the process holding a resource R, P_r be a process requesting the same resource R, and T(P_h) and T(P_r) be their timestamps respectively. The decision to wait or preempt one of the processes is based on the following algorithm:
if T(P_r) < T(P_h) then kill P_r
else wait
Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: The scheme is deadlock-free, but not starvation-free

options.label: B
options.text: The scheme is not deadlock-free, but starvation-free

options.label: C
options.text: The scheme is neither deadlock-free nor starvation-free

options.label: D
options.text: The scheme is both deadlock-free and starvation-free

questions.explanation: Since a process is always killed when its timestamp is smaller than the holder's, no process ever waits indefinitely for a cycle to form, so the scheme is deadlock-free. However, since a killed process restarts with the same timestamp, it can repeatedly be killed by newer holders of the same resource, leading to indefinite postponement (starvation) of that process.

questions.question_text:
Suppose n processes, P1, ..., Pn share m identical resource units, which can be reserved and released one at a time. The maximum resource requirement of process Pi is si where si > 0. Which one of the following is a sufficient condition for ensuring that deadlock does not occur?
(a) for all i, si < m
(b) for all i, si < n
(c) sum(i=1 to n) si < (m + n)
(d) sum(i=1 to n) si < (m * n)
questions.explanation: For the worst-case allocation to not lead to deadlock, each process must be allocated one less than its actual requirement plus there must be at least one extra unit available: sum(si - 1) + 1 <= m, which simplifies to sum(si) < m + n.

If the buffer is full (F=0) and Wait(F) and Wait(S) are interchanged in the producer, the producer will hold S while waiting on F, which will never be signaled since the consumer needs S to proceed, causing deadlock. Interchanging Signal(S) and Signal(F) in the consumer only changes the priority order between producer and next consumer, and does not cause deadlock.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following snapshot of a system running n processes. Process i is holding xi instances of a resource R, for 1 <= i <= n. Currently, all instances of R are occupied. Further, for all i, process i has placed a request for an additional yi instances while holding the xi instances it already has. There are exactly two processes p and q such that yp = yq = 0. Which one of the following can serve as a necessary condition to guarantee that the system is not approaching a deadlock?
(a) min(xp, xq) < max(k != p,q) yk
(b) xp + xq >= max(k != p,q) yk
(c) min(xp, xq) < 1
(d) min(xp, xq) > 1
questions.explanation: Since processes p and q have no pending requests, they can release their held instances (xp + xq total) once any waiting process obtains resources. For no deadlock to occur, this combined amount must be enough to satisfy the largest remaining request among the other processes, i.e., xp + xq >= max(k != p,q) yk.

questions.question_text:
A single processor system has three resource types X, Y, and Z, which are shared by three processes. There are 5 units of each resource type. Consider the following scenario, where the column alloc denotes the number of units of each resource type allocated to each process, and the column request denotes the number of units of each resource type requested by a process in order to complete execution. Which of these processes will finish LAST?
Process P0: alloc(X,Y,Z) = 1,2,1; request(X,Y,Z) = 1,0,3
Process P1: alloc(X,Y,Z) = 2,0,1; request(X,Y,Z) = 0,1,2
Process P2: alloc(X,Y,Z) = 2,2,1; request(X,Y,Z) = 1,2,0

options.label: D
options.text: None of the above, since the system is in a deadlock

questions.explanation: Computing available resources at each step: initially available is (0,1,2), which satisfies P1's request, so P1 finishes and releases its allocation, making available (2,1,3). This satisfies P0's request, so P0 finishes, making available (3,3,4), which satisfies P2's request. Hence the finishing order is P1, P0, P2, so P2 finishes last.

options.label: B
options.text: One of the threads can starve

options.label: C
options.text: Some of the items produced by the producer may be lost

options.label: D
options.text: Values generated and stored in 'x' by the producer will always be consumed before the producer can generate a new value

questions.explanation: Since S starts at 1 and Q at 0, the producer must complete P(S) and produce a value before the consumer can proceed via P(Q), and the producer cannot produce again until the consumer signals V(S) after consuming. This strict alternation guarantees every produced value is consumed before the next one is generated.

questions.question_text: An operating system implements a policy that requires a process to release all resources before making a request for another resource. Select the TRUE statement from the following:

options.label: A
options.text: Both starvation and deadlock can occur

options.label: B
options.text: Starvation can occur but deadlock cannot occur

options.label: C
options.text: Starvation cannot occur but deadlock can occur

options.label: D
options.text: Neither starvation nor deadlock can occur

questions.explanation: This policy eliminates the hold-and-wait condition, one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock, so deadlock cannot occur. However, nothing prevents a process from repeatedly being denied resources in favor of others, so starvation is still possible.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT true of deadlock prevention and deadlock avoidance schemes?

options.label: A
options.text: In deadlock prevention, the request for resources is always granted if the resulting state is safe

options.label: B
options.text: In deadlock avoidance, the request for resources is always granted if the resulting state is safe

options.label: C
options.text: Deadlock avoidance is less restrictive than deadlock prevention

options.label: D
options.text: Deadlock avoidance requires knowledge of resource requirements a priori

questions.explanation: In deadlock prevention, requests may be denied even when the resulting state would be safe, since prevention relies on structural restrictions rather than dynamic safe-state checking; this makes statement (a) false, which is why it is the correct choice for a NOT-true statement.

questions.question_text:
Consider a system with 4 types of resources R1 (3 units), R2 (2 units), R3 (3 units), R4 (2 units). A non-preemptive resource allocation policy is used. At any given instance, a request is not entertained if it cannot be completely satisfied. Three processes P1, P2, P3 request the resources as follows if executed independently.
Process P1: t=0 requests 2 units of R2; t=1 requests 1 unit of R3; t=3 requests 2 units of R1; t=5 releases 1 unit of R2 and 1 unit of R1; t=7 releases 1 unit of R3; t=8 requests 2 units of R4; t=10 Finishes
Process P2: t=0 requests 2 units of R3; t=2 requests 1 unit of R4; t=4 requests 1 unit of R1; t=6 releases 1 unit of R3; t=8 Finishes
Process P3: t=0 requests 1 unit of R4; t=2 requests 2 units of R1; t=5 releases 2 units of R1; t=7 requests 1 unit of R2; t=8 requests 1 unit of R3; t=9 Finishes
Which one of the following statements is TRUE if all three processes run concurrently starting at time t = 0?

options.label: A
options.text: All processes will finish without any deadlock

options.label: B
options.text: Only P1 and P2 will be in deadlock

options.label: C
options.text: Only P1 and P3 will be in deadlock

options.label: D
options.text: All three processes will be in deadlock

questions.explanation: Tracking the available units of each resource type at each timestamp as the three processes request and release resources concurrently shows that every request can eventually be satisfied without any process being blocked indefinitely, so all processes complete without deadlock.

Even-indexed processes always request even-numbered resources and odd-indexed processes always request odd-numbered resources, so if these two sets never overlap, no deadlock can occur. Deadlock becomes possible only when the resource ranges requested by even and odd processes overlap, which happens for n = 21, k = 12.

questions.question_text:
An operating system uses the Banker's algorithm for deadlock avoidance when managing the allocation of three resource types X, Y, and Z to three processes P0, P1, and P2. The table given below presents the current system state. Here, the Allocation matrix shows the current number of resources of each type allocated to each process and the Max matrix shows the maximum number of resources of each type required by each process during its execution.
Allocation(X,Y,Z): P0=0,0,1; P1=3,2,0; P2=2,1,1
Max(X,Y,Z): P0=8,4,3; P1=6,2,0; P2=3,3,3
There are 3 units of type X, 2 units of type Y and 2 units of type Z still available. The system is currently in a safe state. Consider the following independent requests for additional resources in the current state:
REQ1: P0 requests 0 units of X, 0 units of Y and 2 units of Z
REQ2: P1 requests 2 units of X, 0 units of Y and 0 units of Z
Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.label: C
options.text: Both REQ1 and REQ2 can be permitted.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither REQ1 nor REQ2 can be permitted.

questions.explanation: REQ1 would require P0's need to become 8,4,4 which exceeds available resources after allocation and cannot lead to a safe state. REQ2 raises P1's allocation to 5,2,0, after which P1 can complete and release resources, allowing P2 and P0 to eventually complete as well, so only REQ2 keeps the system in a safe state.

questions.question_text: A system contains three programs and each requires three tape units for its operation. The minimum number of tape units which the system must have such that deadlocks never arise is ____
questions.explanation: Using the worst-case allocation formula, allocate one less than the actual requirement to each process plus one extra unit to guarantee no deadlock: (3-1)+(3-1)+(3-1)+1 = 7.

questions.question_text: A system has 6 identical resources and N processes competing for them. Each process can request atmost 2 resources. Which one of the following values of N could lead to a deadlock?
questions.explanation: Deadlock could occur only if N >= 6 (each of N processes holds 1 unit and waits for a second, requiring N >= 6 x (2-1)). None of the given options (1, 2, 3, 4) satisfy this condition, so according to the official answer key no listed option is correct for this question.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following policies for preventing deadlock in a system with mutually exclusive resources.
I. Processes should acquire all their resources at the beginning of execution. If any resource is not available, all resources acquired so far are released.
II. The resources are numbered uniquely, and processes are allowed to request for resources only in increasing resource numbers.
III. The resources are numbered uniquely, and processes are allowed to request for resources only in decreasing resource numbers.
IV. The resources are numbered uniquely. A process is allowed to request only for a resource with resource number larger than its currently held resources.
Which of the above policies can be used for preventing deadlock?

options.label: A
options.text: Any one of I and III but not II or IV

options.label: B
options.text: Any one of I, III and IV but not II

options.label: C
options.text: Any one of II and III but not I or IV

options.label: D
options.text: Any one of I, II, III and IV

questions.explanation: Policy I eliminates hold-and-wait, while policies II, III, and IV each eliminate circular wait by enforcing a strict ordering (increasing or decreasing) on resource requests, so all four policies independently prevent deadlock.

questions.question_text:
A system shares 9 tape drives. The current allocation and maximum requirement of tape drives for three processes are shown below:
Process P1: Current Allocation 3, Maximum Requirement 7
Process P2: Current Allocation 1, Maximum Requirement 6
Process P3: Current Allocation 3, Maximum Requirement 5
Which of the following best describes current state of the system?
questions.explanation: With 9 total drives and 7 currently allocated, 2 remain available. A safe sequence P3, P1, P2 exists since each process's remaining need can be satisfied in turn as drives are released, so the system is both safe and not deadlocked.

questions.question_text: Consider a system with 3 processes that share 4 instances of the same resource type. Each process can request a maximum of K instances. Resource instances can be requested and released only one at a time. The largest value of K that will always avoid deadlock is ____.
questions.explanation: With 3 processes sharing 4 instances, the largest K such that (K-1) x 3 + 1 <= 4 holds is K = 2, guaranteeing deadlock is always avoided.

questions.question_text:
In a system, there are three types of resources: E, F and G. Four processes P0, P1, P2 and P3 execute concurrently. At the outset, the processes have declared their maximum resource requirements using a matrix named Max as given below. For example Max[P2, F] is the maximum number of instances of F that P2 would require. The number of instances of the resources allocated to the various processes at any given state is given by a matrix named Allocation.
Consider a state of the system with the Allocation matrix as shown below and in which 3 instances of E and 3 instances of F are the only resources available.
Allocation(E,F,G): P0=1,0,1; P1=1,1,2; P2=1,0,3; P3=2,0,0
Max(E,F,G): P0=4,3,1; P1=2,1,4; P2=1,3,3; P3=5,4,1
From the perspective of deadlock avoidance, which one of the following is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The system is in safe state.

options.label: B
options.text: The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of E were available.

options.label: C
options.text: The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of F were available.

options.label: D
options.text: The system is not in safe state, but would be safe if one more instance of G were available.

questions.explanation: Computing the need matrix and checking against available resources (3 E, 3 F, and computed G available), a safe sequence P0, P2, P1, P3 exists in which each process's remaining need can be satisfied in turn, so the system is already in a safe state.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to deadlocks?
(a) Circular wait is a necessary condition for the formation of deadlock.
(b) In a system where each resource has more than one instance, a cycle in its wait-for graph indicates the presence of a deadlock.
(c) If the current allocation of resources to processes leads the system to unsafe state, then deadlock will necessarily occur.
(d) In the resource-allocation graph of a system, if every edge is an assignment edge, then the system is not in deadlock state.

options.label: A
options.text: Circular wait is a necessary condition for the formation of deadlock.

options.label: B
options.text: In a system where each resource has more than one instance, a cycle in its wait-for graph indicates the presence of a deadlock.

options.label: C
options.text: If the current allocation of resources to processes leads the system to unsafe state, then deadlock will necessarily occur.

options.label: D
options.text: In the resource-allocation graph of a system, if every edge is an assignment edge, then the system is not in deadlock state.

questions.explanation: Circular wait is indeed one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock, making (a) true. In multi-instance resource systems a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock, making (b) false. An unsafe state does not necessarily lead to deadlock, only makes it possible, so (c) is false. If every edge is an assignment edge, no process is waiting for a resource, so the system cannot be deadlocked, making (d) true.

questions.question_text:
P = {P1, P2, P3, P4} consists of all active processes in an operating system. R = {R1, R2, R3, R4} consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system. The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.
Assignment edges: R1 to P1, R2 to P2, R3 to P3, R4 to P4 (the assignment edge R1 to P1 means resource R1 is assigned to process P1, and so on for others)
Claim edges: P1 to R2, P2 to R3, P3 to R1, P2 to R4, P4 to R2 (the claim edge P1 to R2 means process P1 is waiting for resource R2, and so on for others)
Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?

options.label: A
options.text: Aborting P1 makes the system deadlock free.

options.label: B
options.text: Aborting P3 makes the system deadlock free.

options.label: C
options.text: Aborting P2 makes the system deadlock free.

options.label: D
options.text: Aborting P1 and P4 makes the system deadlock free.

questions.explanation: The graph forms cycles through P1-R2-P2-R3-P3-R1-P1 and involves P4 via P4-R2 and R4-P4. Aborting P2 removes edges that are part of the main cycle, breaking it and making the system deadlock free. Aborting both P1 and P4 together also removes enough edges to eliminate all cycles, so both (c) and (d) are correct, while aborting only P1 or only P3 individually leaves a cycle intact.

questions.question_text:
With respect to deadlocks in an operating system, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
(a) Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks
(b) Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed
(c) An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource
(d) A safe state guarantees that all processes can finish without formation of a deadlock

options.label: A
options.text: Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks

options.label: B
options.text: Deadlock formation can be prevented by ensuring that the hold and wait condition is not allowed

options.label: C
options.text: An assignment edge in a resource allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource

options.label: D
options.text: A safe state guarantees that all processes can finish without formation of a deadlock

questions.explanation: Banker's algorithm is classified as a deadlock avoidance technique, not a prevention technique, so (a) is false. Eliminating hold-and-wait correctly prevents deadlock, so (b) is true. An assignment edge is actually directed from a resource to a process, the reverse of what (c) states, so (c) is false. A safe state by definition guarantees a safe sequence exists in which all processes finish, so (d) is true.

questions.question_text: Consider a system consisting of k instances of a resource R, being shared by 5 processes. Assume that each process requires a maximum of two instances of resource R and a process can request or release only one instance at a time. Further, a process can request the second instance of the resource only after acquiring the first instance. The minimum value of K for the system to be deadlock-free is ____. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Using the worst-case formula m = n x (R-1) + 1 with n = 5 processes and R = 2 maximum instances per process, K = 5 x (2-1) + 1 = 6.

questions.question_text:
When an interrupt occurs, an operating system
(a) ignores the interrupt
(b) always changes state of interrupted process after processing the interrupt
(c) always resumes execution of interrupted process after processing the interrupt
(d) may change state of interrupted process to 'blocked' and schedule another process

options.label: B
options.text: always changes state of interrupted process after processing the interrupt

options.label: C
options.text: always resumes execution of interrupted process after processing the interrupt

options.label: D
options.text: may change state of interrupted process to 'blocked' and schedule another process

questions.explanation: An interrupt is a signal from a device attached to a computer or from a program within the computer that causes the main program that operates the computer to stop and figure out what to do next. After the interrupt signal is sensed, it may change state of interrupted process to 'blocked' and schedule another process.

questions.question_text:
A user level process in Unix traps the signal sent on a Ctrl-C input, and has a signal handling routine that saves appropriate files before terminating the process. When a Ctrl-C input is given to this process, what is the mode in which the signal handling routine executes?
(a) kernel mode
(b) super user mode
(c) privileged mode
(d) user mode
questions.explanation: When user level process trapping the Ctrl+C signal, the trap signal goes through a system call and that's why the mode changes to Kernel mode from user mode and then the request is handled. Kernel mode and privilege mode are the same, so the answer is Kernel mode (privilege mode).

questions.question_text:
A student wishes to create symbolic links in a computer system running Unix. Three text files named "file1", "file2" and "file3" exist in her current working directory, and the student has read and write permissions for all three files. Assume that file1 contains information about her hobbies, file2 contains information about her friends and file3 contains information about her courses. The student executes the following sequence of commands from her current working directory
ln -s file1 file2
ln -s file2 file3
Which of the following types of information would be lost from her file system?
I. Hobbies
II. Friends
III. Courses
(a) I and II only
(b) II and III only
(c) II only
(d) I and III only
questions.explanation: In unix system, the command $ ln -s file1 file2 replaces existing file2 by file1. If file2 exists then it is first removed then replaced with file1. Given: ln -s file1 file2 then ln -s file2 file3. So, file2 replaces file3, then file1 replaces file2, i.e. friends and courses information are lost, and hobbies remain.

questions.question_text:
The shell command
find -name password -print
is executed in /etc directory of a computer system running Unix. Which of the following shell commands will give the same information as the above command when executed in the same directory?
(a) ls passwd
(b) cat passwd
(c) grep name passwd
(d) grep print passwd

Consider n jobs J1, J2, ..., Jn such that job Ji has execution time ti and a non-negative integer weight wi. The weighted mean completion time of the jobs is defined to be (sum_{i=1}^{n} wi*Ti) / (sum_{i=1}^{n} wi) where Ti is the completion time of job Ji. Assuming that there is only one processor available, in what order must the jobs be executed in order to minimize the weighted mean completion time of the jobs?
(a) Non-decreasing order of ti
(b) Non-increasing order of wi
(c) Non-increasing order of wi*ti
(d) Non-increasing order of wi/ti
questions.explanation: To minimize the weighted mean completion time, jobs must be executed in increasing order of weight/time like FCFS scheduling algorithm. If we go with decreasing order of weight/time then it suffers from convoy effect.

questions.question_text:
The correct matching for the following pairs is:
List-I: A. DMA I/O  B. Cache  C. Interrupt I/O  D. Condition Code Register
List-II: 1. High speed RAM  2. Disk  3. Printer  4. ALU
questions.explanation: DMA I/O maps to Disk, Cache maps to High speed RAM, Interrupt I/O maps to Printer, and Condition Code Register maps to ALU.

questions.question_text:

List-I: A. Disk scheduling  B. Batch processing  C. Time sharing  D. Interrupt processing

questions.explanation: Disk scheduling maps to SCAN, Batch processing maps to FIFO (queue), Time sharing maps to Round Robin (uses time slice), and Interrupt processing maps to LIFO (stack).

(a) Hard disk

questions.question_text:
In the index allocation scheme of blocks to a file, the maximum possible size of the file depends on:
(a) the size of the blocks, and the size of the address of the blocks.
(b) the number of blocks used for the index, and the size of the blocks
(c) the size of the blocks, the number of blocks used for the index, and the size of the address of the blocks
(d) None of the above

options.label: A
options.text: the size of the blocks, and the size of the address of the blocks.

options.label: B
options.text: the number of blocks used for the index, and the size of the blocks

options.label: C
options.text: the size of the blocks, the number of blocks used for the index, and the size of the address of the blocks

questions.question_text:
Using a larger block size in a fixed block size file system leads to:
(a) better disk throughput but poorer disk space utilization
(b) better disk throughput and better disk space utilization
(c) poorer disk throughput but better disk space utilization
(d) poorer disk throughput and poorer disk space utilization

options.label: B
options.text: better disk throughput and better disk space utilization

options.label: C
options.text: poorer disk throughput but better disk space utilization

options.label: D
options.text: poorer disk throughput and poorer disk space utilization

questions.explanation: In a fixed block size file system, a larger block size gives better disk throughput but poorer disk space utilization due to increased internal fragmentation.

questions.question_text:
A Unix-style I-node has 10 direct pointers and one single, one double and one triple indirect pointers. Disk block size is 1 Kbyte, disk block address is 32 bits, and 48-bit integers are used. What is the maximum possible file size?
(a) 2^24 bytes
(b) 2^32 bytes
(c) 2^34 bytes
(d) 2^48 bytes
tags: Inode Structure and File Size Calculation
questions.explanation: Number of disk block pointers that fit in one block = 2^10 byte / 4 byte = 256. Maximum file size due to direct pointers = 10 x 1 = 10 KB. Due to single indirection = 256 x 1 = 256 KB. Due to double indirection = 256 x 256 x 1 KB. Due to triple indirection = 256 x 256 x 256 x 1 KB. So maximum file size = 256 x 256 x 256 x 1 KB = 2^8 x 2^8 x 2^8 x 2^10 bytes = 2^24 x 2^10 bytes = 2^34 bytes.

questions.question_text:
A disk has 200 tracks (numbered 0 through 199). At a given time, it was servicing the request of reading data from track 120, and at the previous request, service was for track 90. The pending requests (in order of their arrival) are for track numbers: 30 70 115 130 110 80 20 25. How many times will the head change its direction for the disk scheduling policies SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First) and FCFS (First Come First Serve)?
(a) 2 and 3
(b) 3 and 3
(c) 3 and 4
(d) 4 and 4
questions.explanation: Using FCFS, the head changes direction 4 times while servicing the requests in arrival order. Using SSTF, the head changes direction 3 times, since the head always moves toward the nearest pending request.

questions.question_text:
In a particular Unix OS, each data block is of size 1024 bytes, each node has 10 direct data block addresses and three additional addresses: one for single indirect block, one for double indirect block and one for triple indirect block. Also, each block can contain addresses for 128 blocks. Which one of the following is approximately the maximum size of a file in the file system?
(a) 512 MB
(b) 2 GB
(c) 8 GB
(d) 16 GB
tags: Inode Structure and File Size Calculation
questions.explanation: Maximum file size = [direct data blocks + number of (data block size/DBA) + number of (data block size/DBA)^2 + number of (data block size/DBA)^3] x data block size = [10 + 1x128 + 1x(128x128) + 1x(128x128x128)] x 1024 bytes, which is approximately 2 GB.

questions.question_text:
In a computer system, four files of size 11050 bytes, 4990 bytes, 5170 bytes and 12640 bytes need to be stored. For storing these files on disk, we can use either 100 byte disk blocks or 200 byte disk blocks (but can't mix block sizes). For each block used to store a file, 4 bytes of bookkeeping information also needs to be stored on the disk. A disk block can store either bookkeeping information for a file or data from a file, but not both. What is the total space required for storing the files using 100 byte disk blocks and 200 byte disk blocks respectively?
(a) 35400 and 35800 bytes
(b) 35800 and 35400 bytes
(c) 35600 and 35400 bytes
(d) 35400 and 35600 bytes
questions.explanation: With 200 byte blocks, total blocks needed = 171 and bookkeeping blocks = 6, giving space = (171+6) x 200 = 35400 bytes. With 100 byte blocks, total blocks needed = 340 and bookkeeping blocks = 16, giving space = (340+16) x 100 = 35600 bytes. So the answer is 35600 bytes (100-byte blocks) and 35400 bytes (200-byte blocks).

questions.question_text:
In the working-set strategy, which of the following is done by the operating system to prevent thrashing?
I. It initiates another process if there are enough extra frames.
II. It selects a process to suspend if the sum of the sizes of the working-sets exceeds the total number of available frames.
III. (combined with II as stated)
(a) I only
(b) II only
(c) Neither I nor II
(d) Both I and II
questions.explanation: If the sum of the working-set sizes exceeds the total number of available frames, the operating system selects a process to suspend; its pages are swapped out and its frames reallocated. The suspended process can be restarted later.

questions.question_text:
Directions for Question 5.17 to 5.18: The head of a hard disk serves requests following the shortest seek time first (SSTF) policy. The head is initially positioned at track number 180.
Which of the request sets will cause the head to change its direction after servicing every request, assuming that the head does not change direction if there is a tie in SSTF and all the requests arrive before the servicing starts?
(a) 11, 139, 170, 178, 181, 184, 201, 265
(b) 10, 138, 170, 178, 181, 185, 201, 265
(c) 10, 139, 169, 178, 181, 184, 201, 265
(d) 10, 138, 170, 178, 181, 185, 200, 265
questions.explanation: Starting at 180, the head must first move to 181 since all requests contain it. Checking distances at each step (using the tie-breaking rule that direction does not change on a tie), the sequence 10, 138, 170, 178, 181, 185, 201, 265 causes the head to reverse direction after every request.

questions.question_text:
Directions for Question 5.17 to 5.18: The head of a hard disk serves requests following the shortest seek time first (SSTF) policy. The head is initially positioned at track number 180.
What is the maximum cardinality of the request set, so that the head changes its direction after servicing every request if the total number of tracks are 2048 and the head can start from any track?
(a) 9
(b) 10
(c) 11
(d) 12
questions.explanation: For the head to reverse direction after every request, the distance pattern must follow new_min_distance = (old_distance x 2) + 1, giving the sequence 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, 127, 255, 511, 1023, 2047. This allows a maximum of 11 requests to be satisfied within 2048 tracks.

questions.question_text:
A virtual memory system uses First In First Out (FIFO) page replacement policy and allocates a fixed number of frames to a process. Consider the following statements:
P: Increasing the number of page frames allocated to a process sometimes increases the page fault rate.
Q: Some programs do not exhibit locality of reference.
Which one of the following is TRUE?
(a) Both P and Q are true, and Q is the reason for P
(b) Both P and Q are true, but Q is not the reason for P
(c) P is false, but Q is true
(d) Both P and Q are false

options.label: A
options.text: Both P and Q are true, and Q is the reason for P

options.label: B
options.text: Both P and Q are true, but Q is not the reason for P

options.label: C
options.text: P is false, but Q is true

options.label: D
options.text: Both P and Q are false

questions.explanation: Both P and Q are true, but Q is not the reason for P. Increasing the number of page frames allocated to a process sometimes increases the page fault rate due to Belady's anomaly under FIFO, which is unrelated to whether a program exhibits locality of reference.

questions.question_text:
The data block of a very large file in the Unix file system are allocated using:
(a) Contiguous allocation
(b) Linked allocation
(c) indexed allocation
(d) an extension of indexed allocation
questions.explanation: An extension of indexed allocation (using single, double, and triple indirect blocks) is used to allocate the data blocks of a very large file in the Unix file system.

questions.question_text:
Consider a disk system with 100 cylinders. The requests to access the cylinders occur in the following sequence: 4, 34, 10, 7, 19, 73, 2, 15, 6, 20. Assuming that the head is currently at cylinder 50, what is the time taken to satisfy all requests if it takes 1 ms to move from one cylinder to adjacent one and shortest seek time first policy is used?
(a) 95 ms
(b) 119 ms
(c) 233 ms
(d) 276 ms
questions.explanation: Starting from cylinder 50 and applying SSTF to service requests 4, 34, 10, 7, 19, 73, 2, 15, 6, 20 in nearest-first order, the total head movement is 119 cylinders, taking 119 ms at 1 ms per cylinder.

questions.question_text:
A multilevel page table is preferred in comparison to a single level page table for translating virtual address to physical address because:
(a) it reduces the memory access time to read or write a memory location
(b) it helps to reduce the size of page table needed to implement the virtual address space of a process
(c) it is required by the translation look aside buffer
(d) it helps to reduce the number of page faults in page replacement algorithms.

options.label: A
options.text: it reduces the memory access time to read or write a memory location

options.label: B
options.text: it helps to reduce the size of page table needed to implement the virtual address space of a process

options.label: C
options.text: it is required by the translation look aside buffer

options.label: D
options.text: it helps to reduce the number of page faults in page replacement algorithms.

questions.explanation: A multilevel page table is preferred because it helps reduce the size of the page table needed to implement the virtual address space of a process.

questions.question_text:
A file system with 300 GByte disk uses a file descriptor with 8 direct block addresses, 1 indirect block address and 1 doubly indirect block address. The size of each disk block is 128 Bytes and the size of each disk block address is 8 Bytes. The maximum possible file size in this file system is:
(a) 3 KBytes
(b) 35 KBytes
(c) 280 KBytes
(d) dependent on the size of the disk
tags: Inode Structure and File Size Calculation

options.label: D
options.text: dependent on the size of the disk

questions.explanation: Maximum possible size = [(address pointed by doubly indirect block)^2 + (address pointed by single indirect address) + address pointed by direct addresses] x block size = [(128/8)^2 + (128/8) + 8] x 128 B = [2^8 + 2^4 + 2^3] x 128 B = 32 KB + 2 KB + 1 KB = 35 KB.

questions.question_text: Suppose a disk has 201 cylinders, numbered from 0 to 200. At some time the disk arm is at cylinder 100, and there is a queue of disk access requests for cylinders 30, 85, 90, 100, 105, 110, 135 and 145. If Shortest-Seek Time First (SSTF) is being used for scheduling the disk access, the request for cylinder 90 is serviced after servicing ______ number of requests.
questions.explanation: Starting from cylinder 100, SSTF services the nearest cylinders first: 100 -> 105 -> 110 -> 90. So the request for cylinder 90 is serviced after servicing 3 requests.

questions.question_text: A FAT (file allocation table) based file system is being used and the total overhead of each entry in the FAT is 4 bytes in size. Given a 100 x 10^6 bytes disk on which the file system is stored and data block size is 10^3 bytes, the maximum size of a file that can be stored on this disk in units of 10^6 bytes is ______.
questions.explanation: Overhead per entry in FAT is 4 bytes, and block size is 1000 bytes, so total size per entry is 1004 bytes. Number of entries in FAT = (100x10^6)/1004 = 0.099601 x 10^6 approximately. Maximum file size = 0.099601 x 10^3 bytes per entry x number of entries, which works out to approximately 99.6 x 10^6 bytes.

questions.question_text: Suppose the following disk request sequence (track numbers) for a disk with 100 tracks is given: 45, 20, 90, 10, 50, 60, 80, 25, 70. Assume that the initial position of the R/W head is on track 50. The additional distance that will be traversed by the R/W head when the Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) algorithm is used compared to the SCAN (Elevator) algorithm (assuming that SCAN algorithm moves towards 100 when it starts execution) is ______ tracks.
questions.explanation: SSTF total head movement = (50-45)+(90-45)+(90-10) = 5+45+80 = 130. SCAN total head movement = (90-50)+(90-10) = 40+80 = 120. Difference = 130 - 120 = 10 tracks.

questions.question_text: Consider a disk queue with requests for I/O to blocks on cylinders 47, 38, 121, 191, 87, 11, 92, 10. The C-LOOK scheduling algorithm is used. The head is initially at cylinder number 63, moving towards larger cylinder numbers on its servicing pass. The cylinders are numbered from 0 to 199. The total head movement (in number of cylinders) incurred while servicing these requests is ______.

In a file allocation system, which of the following allocation scheme(s) can be used if no external fragmentation is allowed?
I. Contiguous
II. Linked
III. Indexed
(a) I and III only
(b) II only
(c) III only
(d) II and III only
questions.explanation: Linked and indexed allocations are non-contiguous, so they do not suffer from external fragmentation, unlike contiguous allocation.

questions.question_text: Consider a storage disk with 4 platters (numbered as 0, 1, 2 and 3), 200 cylinders (numbered as 0, 1, ....., 199) and 256 sectors per track (numbered as 0, 1, ....., 255). The following 6 disk requests of the form [sector number, cylinder number, platter number] are received by the disk controller at the same time: [120, 72, 2], [180, 134, 1], [60, 20, 0], [212, 86, 3], [56, 116, 2], [118, 16, 1]. Currently the head is positioned at sector number 100 of cylinder 80 and is moving towards higher cylinder numbers. The average power dissipation in moving the head over 100 cylinders is 20 milliwatts and for reversing the direction of the head movement once is 15 milliwatts. Power dissipation associated with rotational latency and switching of head between different platters is negligible. The total power consumption in milliwatts to satisfy all of the above disk requests using the Shortest Seek Time First disk scheduling algorithm is ______.
questions.explanation: Using SSTF on cylinder numbers 72, 134, 20, 86, 116, 16 starting from 80: total cylinder movement = (86-80)+(86-72)+(134-72)+(134-16) = 6+14+62+118 = 200 cylinders, with 3 direction reversals. Power = (200/100)x20 + 3x15 = 40 + 45 = 85 milliwatts.

questions.question_text: The index node (inode) of a Unix-like file system has 12 direct, one single-indirect and one double-indirect pointers. The disk block size is 4 kB and the disk block address is 32-bits long. The maximum possible file size is (rounded off to 1 decimal place) ______ GB.
tags: Inode Structure and File Size Calculation
questions.explanation: Disk block size = 4 kB, disk block address = 32 bit = 4 B. Number of addresses in one disk block = 4kB/4B = 2^10. With 12 direct, 1 single indirect, and 1 double indirect pointer, maximum possible file size = (12 + 2^10 + 2^10 x 2^10) x 4 kB = 4.00395 GB, approximately 4 GB.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following five disk access requests of the form (request id, cylinder number) that are present in the disk scheduler queue at a given time: (P, 155), (Q, 85), (R, 110), (S, 30), (T, 115). Assume the head is positioned at cylinder 100. The scheduler follows Shortest Seek Time First scheduling to service the requests. Which one of the following statements is FALSE?
(a) R is serviced before P.
(b) T is serviced before P.
(c) Q is serviced after S but before T.
(d) The head reverses its direction of movement between servicing of Q and P.

options.label: C
options.text: Q is serviced after S but before T.

options.label: D
options.text: The head reverses its direction of movement between servicing of Q and P.

questions.explanation: Applying SSTF from cylinder 100, the servicing order is R(110), T(115), Q(85), S(30), P(155). So P is serviced last, making statements (a) and (b) true, and the head does reverse direction between Q and P, making (d) true. However, Q is actually serviced before S, not after, so statement (c) is FALSE.

questions.question_text:
Consider a linear list based directory implementation in a file system. Each directory is a list of nodes, where each node contains the file name along with the file metadata, such as the list of pointers to the data blocks. Consider a given directory foo. Which of the following operations will necessarily require a full scan of foo for successful completion?
(a) Opening of an existing file in foo
(b) Renaming of an existing file in foo
(c) Creation of a new file in foo
(d) Deletion of an existing file from foo

options.label: A
options.text: Opening of an existing file in foo

options.label: B
options.text: Renaming of an existing file in foo

options.label: C
options.text: Creation of a new file in foo

options.label: D
options.text: Deletion of an existing file from foo

questions.explanation: Renaming a file requires a full scan to check for name conflicts and locate the entry, and creating a new file requires a full scan to ensure a duplicate name does not already exist.

questions.question_text: Consider two files systems A and B, that use contiguous allocation and linked allocation, respectively. A file of size 100 blocks is already stored in A and also in B. Now, consider inserting a new block in the middle of the file (between 50th and 51st block), whose data is already available in the memory. Assume that there are enough free blocks at the end of the file and that the file control blocks are already in memory. Let the number of disk accesses required to insert a block in the middle of the file in A and B are n_A and n_B, respectively, then the value of n_A + n_B is ______.
questions.explanation: For contiguous allocation (A): 50 read operations + 50 write operations + 1 operation to write the newly inserted block = 101 operations. For linked allocation (B): 50 read operations + 1 operation to update the next pointer of the 50th element + 1 operation to connect it to the 51st element = 52 operations. Total = 101 + 52 = 153.

questions.question_text: Consider a 512 GB hard disk with 32 storage surfaces. There are 4096 sectors per track and each sector holds 1024 bytes of data. The number of cylinders in the hard disk is ______.
questions.explanation: Disk capacity = number of surfaces x number of tracks per surface x number of sectors per track x number of bytes per sector. 512 GB = 32 x x x 4096 x 1024 B, i.e., 2^39 B = 2^5 x x x 2^12 x 2^10 B, so 2^39 = 2^27 x, giving x = 2^12 = 4096.

questions.question_text: Consider a disk with the following specifications: rotation speed of 6000 RPM, average seek time of 5 milliseconds, 500 sectors/track, 512 byte sectors. A file has content stored in 3000 sectors located randomly on the disk. Assuming average rotational latency, the total time (in seconds, rounded off to 2 decimal places) to read the entire file from the disk is ______.
questions.explanation: Average seek time = 5 ms. Time per revolution = 60/6000 sec = 10 ms, so average rotational latency = 10/2 = 5 ms. Time to read one sector = 10 ms / 500 sectors = 0.02 ms. Average time per sector access = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time = 5+5+0.02 = 10.02 ms. For 3000 sectors, total time = 10.02 x 3000 = 30060 ms = 30.06 seconds.

questions.question_text: A disk of size 512 M bytes is divided into blocks of 64 K bytes. A file is stored in the disk using linked allocation. In linked allocation, each data block reserves 4 bytes to store the pointer to the next data block. The link part of the last data block contains a NULL pointer (also of 4 bytes). Suppose a file of 1 M bytes needs to be stored in the disk. Assume, 1 K = 2^10 and 1 M = 2^20. The amount of space in bytes that will be wasted due to internal fragmentation is ______. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation: Block size = 64 K = 65536 bytes. Usable data per block = 65536 - 4 = 65532 bytes. Number of blocks needed = 1 MB / 65532 = 16.007, so 16 blocks are used, storing 16 x 65532 = 1048512 bytes. Remaining data to store = 1048576 - 1048512 = 64 bytes, which goes into the last block along with its 4-byte NULL pointer, using 68 bytes of the 65536-byte block. Wasted space in the last block = 65536 - 68 = 65468 bytes.

questions.question_text:
To keep track of free blocks in a file system, one of the two approaches is generally used - using bitmaps (bit vectors) or using linked lists. Consider that the linked list approach is used to keep track of free blocks in a file system. Assume that the disk size is 16 GB, block size is 2 KB, and block numbers used are 32-bit long. A single pointer of size 4 bytes is used in each block of the list to point to the next block of the list. The number of blocks required to hold the free disk block numbers is ______. (answer in integer)
Note: 1K = 2^10 and 1G = 2^30
questions.explanation: Total number of disk blocks = disk size / block size = 16 GB / 2 KB = 2^34/2^11 = 2^23 = 8388608. Each free list block stores block numbers plus 1 pointer, so usable space for block numbers per block = 2048 - 4 = 2044 bytes, giving 2044/4 = 511 block numbers per block. Total free list blocks required = ceil(8388608 / 511) = 16417.

questions.question_text: The process of assigning load addresses to the various parts of the program and adjusting the code and data in the program to reflect the assigned addresses is called
questions.explanation: Relocation can change the assigned address of data and code in the program.

questions.question_text: Consider a virtual memory system with FIFO page replacement policy. For an arbitrary page access pattern, increasing the number of page frames in main memory will

options.label: A
options.text: always decrease the number of page faults

options.label: B
options.text: always increase the number of page faults

options.label: C
options.text: sometimes increase the number of page faults

options.label: D
options.text: never affect the number of page faults

questions.explanation: Belady's Anomaly: increasing the number of frames can sometimes increase the number of page faults, and this is observed with the FIFO replacement policy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a form of memory?
questions.explanation: Instruction cache, instruction register, and TLB are memories, but instruction opcode is the part of an instruction that specifies the operation to perform.

questions.question_text: The optimal page replacement algorithm will, select the page that

options.label: A
options.text: Has not been used for the longest time in the past

options.label: B
options.text: Will not be used for the longest time in the future

options.label: C

options.label: D
